title: Monopoly
in30Seconds: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry. Because it is the only supplier, the monopolist faces the whole downward-sloping market demand curve and is a price maker: to sell more it must lower the price on every unit, so its marginal revenue falls below the price. It maximizes profit at the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then charges the highest price the demand curve allows there, producing less and charging more than a competitive market would.
whyItMatters: Market structure decides who holds power over price, and monopoly is the extreme case where one firm sets it. The model explains why a single seller produces less and charges more than a competitive industry, and why economists call part of that gap a deadweight loss rather than a simple transfer from buyers to the firm. The same logic drives real debates: how patents trade higher prices now for more invention later, why electricity and water utilities are regulated instead of broken into competitors, and when antitrust authorities challenge a merger. Knowing the mechanics lets you weigh those arguments on evidence, and it anchors the comparison with the other market structures you will study next.
learningObjectives: Define monopoly and identify the barriers to entry, legal, natural (economies of scale), control of a key resource, and network effects, that protect it.
Explain why a monopolist is a price maker facing the market demand curve and why its marginal revenue lies below the price.
Apply the MR = MC rule to find a monopolist's profit-maximizing quantity and read the corresponding price off the demand curve.
Analyze why monopoly yields lower output at a higher price than perfect competition, and why this produces a deadweight loss.
Distinguish a natural monopoly, explain the basic case for regulating it, and identify price discrimination.

collegeVersion.heading: Barriers to entry: what makes a market a monopoly
collegeVersion.body:
A monopoly is a market served by a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes. The word describes the whole market, not just a big firm: if buyers who dislike the price have nowhere else to turn, the seller has genuine market power. What keeps that position from being competed away is a barrier to entry, a legal, technological, or market force that discourages or prevents potential rivals from entering. Without such a barrier, the profits a lone seller earns would attract new firms until the extra competition eroded them, so barriers are what let a monopoly persist.

Barriers come in a few recognizable forms. Legal barriers are created by government: a patent gives an inventor the exclusive right to make, use, or sell an invention for a limited time (20 years in the United States), and trademarks and copyrights work similarly, while some statutes grant an outright legal monopoly, such as the U.S. Postal Service's exclusive right to deliver first-class mail. A natural monopoly arises from technology and cost: when economies of scale are large relative to the size of the market, one firm can supply the entire quantity demanded at a lower average cost than two or more firms could, as with the pipes and wires of water and electric utilities. Control of a scarce key resource can also block entry; historically ALCOA controlled the bauxite needed for aluminum, and De Beers long dominated the supply of rough diamonds. Network effects can act as a modern barrier, because a product that becomes more valuable as more people use it is hard for a newcomer to displace. This lesson owns monopoly; oligopoly and monopolistic competition, the in-between structures, are named here and taught in their own lessons.

collegeVersion.heading: The demand curve a monopoly faces, and why marginal revenue is below price
collegeVersion.body:
The single most important difference between a monopoly and a competitive firm is the demand curve each one faces. A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: it is so small relative to the market that it can sell all it wants at the going price, so the demand curve for its own output is effectively a flat line at that price. A monopoly is the entire industry, so it faces the whole market demand curve, which slopes downward. That single fact makes the monopolist a price maker: it can choose a higher price and sell less, or a lower price and sell more, but it cannot have both. Every price-quantity pair it might pick is a point on that one demand curve.

Because the curve slopes down, selling one more unit requires cutting the price, and for a single-price seller that cut applies to every unit, not just the last one. So the marginal revenue from an extra unit, the change in total revenue, has two parts: the firm gains the price of the new unit, but it loses a little on each earlier unit that now sells for less. The loss on the earlier units drags marginal revenue below the price. Marginal revenue therefore lies beneath the demand curve at every quantity past the first. This is not a minor technicality; it is the hinge of the whole model, because the firm's output decision is driven by marginal revenue, while the price it can charge is read from the higher demand curve. Deriving the underlying cost curves is the job of the costs lesson; here we take marginal cost as given and focus on how revenue behaves.

collegeVersion.heading: Choosing output and price: MR = MC, then read the price off demand
collegeVersion.body:
A monopolist maximizes profit the same way any firm does, by weighing the revenue and the cost of one more unit. As long as an extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, that is, marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, producing it raises profit; once marginal cost would exceed marginal revenue, the firm stops. Profit is largest at the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost: MR = MC. Notice that this rule picks a quantity, not a price.

To find the price, the monopolist takes that profit-maximizing quantity up to the demand curve and charges the most buyers are willing to pay for it. That price sits on the demand curve, which lies above marginal revenue, and marginal revenue was set equal to marginal cost, so the price ends up above marginal cost. This is the defining signature of monopoly, and the one-line contrast with perfect competition captures it: a competitive market is pushed to price equal to marginal cost (P = MC), while a monopoly settles at price greater than marginal cost (P > MC). The monopolist is not charging "as much as possible"; a price too high would sell too little to be profitable. It is charging exactly the price that the MR = MC quantity commands on the demand curve. A monopoly earning profits can keep them precisely because barriers to entry keep rivals out; the same profits in a competitive market would invite entry that competed the price down.

collegeVersion.heading: Why monopoly costs society: deadweight loss, natural monopoly, price discrimination
collegeVersion.body:
Because a monopoly stops where MR = MC rather than where price equals marginal cost, it produces less than the allocatively efficient quantity. Allocative efficiency is the output at which the price buyers place on the last unit just equals the marginal cost of making it; every unit whose value to buyers exceeds its cost of production is worth making. A monopoly leaves some of those mutually beneficial units unproduced, and the value society loses on them, gains that go to neither the buyer nor the seller, is the deadweight loss. It is important to separate this from the higher price on the units that are sold: that higher price transfers surplus from consumers to the firm, but a transfer is not a loss to society, whereas the deadweight loss is surplus that simply vanishes.

The natural-monopoly case is the important exception to the usual policy instinct. When one firm can serve the whole market more cheaply than several could, forcing competition would raise average costs, so governments typically allow a single regulated provider, as with electricity and water, and control its prices rather than break it up. Another wrinkle is price discrimination, charging different buyers different prices for the same good (student and senior discounts are everyday examples). Price discrimination can expand the quantity sold and shrink the deadweight loss, because some buyers who would not pay the single monopoly price are now served, though it tends to shift surplus toward the seller. The broader takeaway is that market structure, not the seller's character, drives these outcomes: change the barriers to entry and you change the price, the quantity, and the efficiency of the whole market.

vocabulary.definition: A market structure in which a single firm is the only seller of a product that has no close substitutes.
A legal, technological, or market force that discourages or prevents potential competitors from entering a market, allowing a monopoly to persist.
A situation in which economies of scale are so large relative to market demand that a single firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than several firms could.
A seller that faces a downward-sloping demand curve and so must choose a point on it, trading a higher price against a lower quantity; contrasted with a price taker.
The change in a firm's total revenue from selling one more unit of output.
The additional cost of producing one more unit of output.
The output level at which the price buyers place on the last unit equals its marginal cost, so all mutually beneficial units are produced.
The loss of total surplus that occurs when output is held below the allocatively efficient level, representing gains from trade that go to neither buyers nor sellers.
Charging different buyers different prices for the same product, based on differences in their willingness to pay.
The tendency for a firm's average cost per unit to fall as its scale of output rises, often because large fixed costs are spread over more units.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine you are the only lemonade stand allowed on the whole street, and a fence keeps anyone else from opening one. You get to pick the price, but there is a catch: the whole street shares one demand list, so to sell more cups you have to drop the price for everybody, not just the next customer. That is why earning an extra sale is worth less than the sticker price to you, because you give up a few coins on all the cups you could have charged more for. So you do not sell as many cups as you could. You pick the amount where the money from one more cup just covers what it costs to make, then charge the highest price that many cups will sell for. The result is fewer cups sold at a higher price than if lots of stands were competing. Some thirsty people who would happily pay more than a cup costs to make never get one, and that missed win is pure waste, not money moved around, just gone.
eli10.analogy: A monopoly is like the only bridge across a river. The bridge owner can set any toll, but a higher toll means fewer cars cross, so there is always a trade-off between the toll and the traffic. The owner picks the toll that makes the most money, and it leaves the bridge emptier than a free-flowing road would be, with some travelers who would gladly pay a fair toll turned away.
eli10.analogyLimits: The bridge makes the single-seller idea vivid, but a real monopolist usually charges one price to everyone at once rather than negotiating car by car, and the analogy hides where the barrier comes from, a patent, a resource, or huge fixed costs, which is exactly what determines whether the monopoly can last.

workedExample: Suppose a firm is the only seller of a patented gadget, and the market demand schedule is P = 11 - Q (in dollars). Its marginal cost is a constant $4 per unit. Build the revenue table: at Q = 1 the price is $10 and total revenue is $10; at Q = 2, price $9, revenue $18, so marginal revenue is $8; at Q = 3, price $8, revenue $24, MR $6; at Q = 4, price $7, revenue $28, MR $4; at Q = 5, price $6, revenue $30, MR $2. Notice marginal revenue is below the price at every step, exactly as the model predicts. The profit-maximizing rule is MR = MC, and MR equals the $4 marginal cost at Q = 4. So the monopolist makes 4 units and reads the price off the demand curve: P = 11 - 4 = $7. Price ($7) exceeds marginal cost ($4), the monopoly signature. An efficient market would keep producing until price met marginal cost, at P = $4, Q = 7. The three units between Q = 4 and Q = 7 are worth more to buyers than they cost to make, yet go unproduced; that forgone surplus is the deadweight loss.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking a monopolist can charge any price it likes with no limit.
commonMistakes.correction: The monopolist still faces the market demand curve. A higher price always means a lower quantity sold, so it is constrained to points on that curve and picks the one that maximizes profit, not the highest number it can imagine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting price where MR = MC.
commonMistakes.correction: MR = MC determines the profit-maximizing quantity, not the price. The price is then read upward from that quantity to the demand curve, and it lies above marginal revenue and marginal cost.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing marginal revenue equals the price for a monopoly, as it does for a price taker.
commonMistakes.correction: Because the demand curve slopes down and one price applies to all units, selling more lowers the price on every unit, so marginal revenue is below the price for a single-price monopolist.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the entire gap between the monopoly price and marginal cost a loss to society.
commonMistakes.correction: The higher price on units actually sold is a transfer from consumers to the firm, not a social loss. The deadweight loss is only the value of the beneficial units that go unproduced because output is restricted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every monopoly should be broken up into competing firms.
commonMistakes.correction: A natural monopoly serves the whole market at lower average cost than several firms could, so splitting it up would raise costs. The usual response is to allow one provider and regulate it, as with electricity and water utilities.

compareContrast.distinction: A monopolist is a price maker facing the whole downward-sloping demand curve and settles at price greater than marginal cost (P > MC); a competitive firm is a price taker and the market is driven to price equal to marginal cost (P = MC).

compareContrast.b: Transfer from consumers to the firm
compareContrast.distinction: The deadweight loss is surplus that vanishes because beneficial units go unproduced; the higher price on units still sold merely moves surplus from buyers to the seller and is not a net loss to society.
A natural monopoly arises from economies of scale that make one firm the cheapest supplier; a legal monopoly is created directly by government through patents, licenses, or statute.

keyTakeaway: A monopoly is a single seller shielded by barriers to entry; facing the whole market demand curve it is a price maker whose marginal revenue lies below price, so it produces where MR = MC and charges a price above marginal cost, yielding less output at a higher price than competition and a deadweight loss to society.

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following best defines a monopoly?
options: A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry
A market with a few large firms that must anticipate one another's decisions
A market with many firms selling slightly differentiated versions of a product
Any firm that earns an economic profit in a given year
questionBank.explanation: A monopoly is a single seller of a good with no close substitutes, kept in place by barriers to entry. A few interdependent firms describes oligopoly, and many firms with differentiated products describes monopolistic competition, both separate structures. Earning a profit for a year does not make a firm a monopoly, since competitive firms can earn short-run profits too.
questionBank.skill: Defining monopoly

questionBank.prompt: A city grants a single company the exclusive right to run water pipes because one firm can supply the whole city at a lower average cost than several competing firms could. This barrier to entry is an example of a:
options: Control of a key physical resource
Natural monopoly arising from economies of scale
Network effect that grows with the number of users
Predatory pricing strategy aimed at rivals
questionBank.explanation: When economies of scale are large relative to market demand, one firm serves the market at lower average cost than many could, which is the definition of a natural monopoly. It is not control of a resource (no scarce input is being cornered), not a network effect (value here comes from scale of production, not from more users), and not predatory pricing (no firm is slashing prices to drive out a rival).
questionBank.skill: Classifying barriers to entry

questionBank.prompt: A single-price monopolist faces demand P = 11 - Q and has a constant marginal cost of $4. Using the rule that it produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, what quantity does it produce and what price does it charge?
options: Q = 7 and P = $4, where price equals marginal cost
Q = 5 and P = $6, the midpoint of the schedule
Q = 6 and P = $5, where marginal revenue is zero
Q = 4 and P = $7, where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
questionBank.explanation: Marginal revenue falls faster than price: at Q = 4 the marginal revenue is $4, equal to marginal cost, so the firm makes 4 units and reads the price off demand, P = 11 - 4 = $7. Q = 7, P = $4 is the efficient competitive outcome where price equals marginal cost, not the monopoly choice. Q = 6 is where marginal revenue hits zero (revenue is maximized, not profit), and Q = 5, P = $6 is not a marginal-revenue-equals-marginal-cost point.
questionBank.skill: Applying MR = MC to find monopoly quantity and price

questionBank.prompt: Compared with a perfectly competitive market for the same good and the same costs, why does economists' analysis say a single-price monopoly imposes a deadweight loss on society?
options: Because the monopoly earns an economic profit, and all profit is a loss to consumers
Because the monopoly restricts output below the level where price equals marginal cost, so some units worth more to buyers than they cost to make are never produced
Because the monopoly always sets price equal to marginal cost, eliminating its own profit
Because the monopoly's marginal revenue lies above its demand curve, raising costs
questionBank.explanation: The deadweight loss comes from restricted output: the monopoly stops where MR = MC, short of where price equals marginal cost, so mutually beneficial units go unproduced and that surplus vanishes. Profit itself is a transfer from consumers to the firm, not a social loss, so the first option is wrong. A monopoly sets price above marginal cost, not equal to it, and its marginal revenue lies below, not above, the demand curve.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the source of monopoly deadweight loss

questionBank.prompt: A monopolist begins offering student and senior discounts, charging those buyers a lower price than everyone else for the same product. What is this practice called, and what is one likely effect?
options: A network effect; it makes the product more valuable as more people buy it
A natural monopoly; it lowers the firm's average cost of production
Price discrimination; it can expand the quantity sold and shrink the deadweight loss while shifting surplus toward the seller
Predatory pricing; it is designed to bankrupt competing firms
questionBank.explanation: Charging different buyers different prices for the same good based on willingness to pay is price discrimination; by serving buyers who would not pay the single monopoly price, it can raise total quantity and reduce the deadweight loss, while moving surplus toward the seller. It is not a network effect (that concerns value rising with users), not a natural monopoly (a cost condition, not a pricing tactic), and not predatory pricing (which targets rivals, not different customer groups).
questionBank.skill: Identifying price discrimination and its effects

title: Oligopoly
in30Seconds: An oligopoly is a market run by just a few large firms, each big enough that its choices about price and output visibly affect the others. That mutual interdependence is the whole story: every firm has to guess how rivals will react before it moves. Firms are tempted to collude, quietly agreeing to hold output down and prices up, but each partner also has a private incentive to cheat, which is why cartels are unstable and, when explicit, usually illegal. Game theory's prisoner's dilemma captures the tension exactly.
whyItMatters: Some of the markets you deal with every day are oligopolies: wireless carriers, airlines, soft drinks, credit-card networks, and commercial aircraft are all controlled by a handful of firms. Understanding oligopoly explains behavior that looks strange under simple supply and demand, like prices that stay stubbornly similar across rivals, sudden price wars, heavy brand advertising, and the recurring headlines about price-fixing prosecutions. It also introduces game theory, a way of reasoning about any situation where your best move depends on what someone else does, which reaches far beyond economics into business strategy, negotiation, politics, and law. Learning why cartels form and why they fall apart gives you a durable tool for reading markets, and for spotting when coordination among competitors has crossed into illegal collusion.
learningObjectives: Define oligopoly as a market dominated by a few large, interdependent firms protected by barriers to entry.
Explain why oligopolies form, drawing on barriers to entry and economies of scale.
Explain mutual interdependence and why it forces firms to behave strategically.
Distinguish collusion and cartels from independent competition, and explain why cartels are both unstable and often illegal.
Apply the prisoner's dilemma to show why rational firms defect from a collusive agreement.
Distinguish oligopoly from monopoly, monopolistic competition, and perfect competition.

collegeVersion.heading: What makes a market an oligopoly
collegeVersion.body: An oligopoly is a market in which a small number of large firms make all or most of the sales. Think of commercial aircraft (essentially Boeing and Airbus), wireless carriers, or the handful of companies that dominate soft drinks, airlines, and cable service. The defining feature is not a magic number of firms but the fact that each firm is large enough for its decisions to matter to the others. Oligopolies form for two main reasons. The first is barriers to entry, the same forces that can create a monopoly: patents, control of a scarce input, high startup costs, or a strong incumbent brand that a newcomer would have to spend enormous sums to challenge. The second is economies of scale. When the lowest-cost way to produce requires such large volume that total market demand can only support a few firms operating efficiently, extra entrants would each produce too little to get their costs down, so the market naturally settles into a few big players. Economists gauge how concentrated a market is with tools such as the four-firm concentration ratio (the combined market share of the largest four firms) and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, or HHI, which squares each firm's market share and adds them up so that dominance by a few firms produces a high number. U.S. antitrust agencies use the HHI in merger review; under the 2023 Merger Guidelines a market is treated as 'highly concentrated' when the post-merger HHI is above 1,800. It helps to place oligopoly among the four standard market structures: perfect competition has many firms selling identical products; monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products; oligopoly has a few interdependent firms; and monopoly has a single firm. This lesson owns only oligopoly; the other three are separate topics.

collegeVersion.heading: Mutual interdependence and strategic behavior
collegeVersion.body: The idea that ties the whole topic together is mutual interdependence. In perfect competition a firm is so small that it can ignore everyone else and simply take the market price. In an oligopoly the opposite is true: because there are only a few firms, one firm's move to cut price, expand output, or launch an advertising blitz noticeably changes the sales and profits of its rivals, who will respond. That means no firm can plan in isolation. Before it acts, each firm has to anticipate how the others will react, and it knows the others are doing the same thing about it. This is what economists mean by strategic behavior: choosing your action based on your best guess of others' responses. Interdependence explains several patterns that look puzzling under textbook supply and demand. Rival gas stations or airlines often post nearly identical prices, not necessarily because they conspired, but because each watches the others and knows a price cut will be matched, erasing any advantage while lowering everyone's revenue. It also explains why oligopolists compete so heavily through advertising, branding, and product features rather than price: non-price competition is harder for a rival to instantly copy, and it avoids triggering a mutually destructive price war. Because the analysis is fundamentally about action and reaction between a few players, ordinary demand-and-supply curves are not enough; the right tool is game theory, which we reach shortly.

collegeVersion.heading: Collusion, cartels, and the law
collegeVersion.body: Since head-to-head competition drives prices and profits down, oligopolists are tempted to do the opposite of compete: to collude. Collusion means firms act together to restrict output and keep prices high, capturing something closer to the profit a single monopolist would earn and splitting it among themselves. When the agreement is formal and explicit, the group is called a cartel. The most famous international example is OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, founded in September 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela; its members meet to assign each country an output quota designed to hold oil prices above the competitive level. OPEC also illustrates the central weakness of every cartel: it is unstable. Once partners agree to keep output low and prices high, each individual member can earn even more by quietly producing beyond its quota and selling the extra at the high price everyone else is propping up. If enough members cheat, output rises and the high price collapses. OPEC members have in fact routinely exceeded their quotas, which is exactly why the cartel's control over prices has always been shaky. In most of the economy there is a second reason cartels are fragile: they are illegal. Under U.S. antitrust law, price fixing, an agreement among competitors to raise, lower, or stabilize prices, is treated as almost always unlawful, and an agreement to restrict output is just as illegal because cutting supply drives prices up. Penalties are serious: individuals can face up to ten years in prison and companies fines up to $100 million (or twice the gain or loss). A vivid case is the lysine conspiracy of the mid-1990s, in which Archer Daniels Midland and several international rivals secretly agreed to fix the price of lysine, a livestock feed additive, raising it roughly 70 percent in the first nine months. The FBI recorded the meetings, where an ADM executive summed up the mindset with the line that their competitors were their friends and their customers were the enemy. ADM pleaded guilty and paid $100 million in fines, then a record, and several executives went to prison. Because explicit collusion is illegal, real oligopolists more often engage in tacit collusion, parallel behavior with no written agreement, which is far harder to prosecute but also far harder to sustain.

collegeVersion.heading: Game theory and the prisoner's dilemma
collegeVersion.body: Game theory is the study of strategic decisions, situations where each player's best choice depends on what the others do. Its most famous example, the prisoner's dilemma, captures the cartel's problem precisely. Imagine two firms, A and B, that together could hold output low and keep prices high. Each faces a simple choice: cooperate (stick to low output) or defect (secretly raise output to grab extra sales). Suppose that if both cooperate, each earns $8 million; if both defect and flood the market, the price falls and each earns only $3 million. But if one defects while the other keeps cooperating, the defector grabs sales worth $10 million while the loyal firm, stuck at a high price nobody is honoring, earns just $1 million. Now reason as firm A. If B cooperates, A earns $10 million by defecting versus $8 million by cooperating, so A should defect. If B defects, A earns $3 million by defecting versus $1 million by cooperating, so A should still defect. Defecting is better no matter what B does; economists call that a dominant strategy. B reasons identically. So both defect and land at $3 million each, even though both would have been better off at $8 million by cooperating. That gap is the dilemma: individually rational choices produce a collectively worse outcome, and it is exactly why a cartel that everyone would benefit from tends to fall apart. In the real world firms play this game repeatedly, which opens the door to sustaining cooperation through strategies like tit-for-tat, matching a rival's cooperation with cooperation and punishing a price cut with an immediate price cut of your own. The threat of retaliation can make honesty the more profitable long-run choice, but it never fully removes each firm's private temptation to cheat.

vocabulary.definition: A market structure in which a few large firms account for most or all of the sales, so each firm's decisions noticeably affect the others.
Something that makes it hard or costly for new firms to enter a market, such as patents, high startup costs, or a dominant brand, protecting incumbent firms.
Cost advantages a firm gains as it produces at higher volume, so that average cost per unit falls; when large, they leave room for only a few efficient firms.
The condition in an oligopoly where each firm's best decision about price, output, or advertising depends on how the other firms are expected to respond.
Firms coordinating their actions, typically to restrict output and keep prices higher than competition would allow.
A group of firms bound by a formal agreement to collude, for example by assigning output quotas to hold prices up.
An agreement among competitors to raise, lower, maintain, or stabilize prices; it is treated as almost always illegal under U.S. antitrust law.
The study of strategic decision-making, in which each player's best choice depends on the choices of the other players.
A game in which each player has an incentive to defect regardless of what the other does, so both defect and end up worse off than if they had cooperated.
A choice that yields a better payoff for a player than any alternative, no matter what the other players decide to do.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: An oligopoly is a market with only a few big sellers, like the two companies that build almost all the world's big passenger jets. Because there are so few of them, each one is huge, and whatever one does, the others feel it right away. So before any of them changes a price, it has to think, 'What will the others do back to me?' They would all make more money if they secretly agreed to keep prices high together. But there is a catch: each one could make even more money by cheating on the deal and selling a little cheaper to steal customers. Since every firm is tempted to cheat, these secret deals keep falling apart, and making such a deal on purpose is usually against the law.
eli10.analogy: It is like a few kids who run all the lemonade stands on one street. If they all quietly agree to charge $2, they each make good money. But any one of them can make more by sneaking their price down to $1.50 to grab the whole line, so somebody always cheats and the deal collapses.
eli10.analogyLimits: The lemonade street is missing two real forces. First, real companies compete hard in ways besides price, spending heavily on advertising and brands to win customers without starting a price war. Second, price-fixing agreements between real companies are illegal and can send executives to prison, while kids agreeing on lemonade prices are not committing a crime.

workedExample: Picture two firms, A and B, that supply most of a market and are deciding whether to keep output low (cooperate, holding prices high) or flood the market (defect). If both keep output low, each earns $8 million. If both flood the market, the price crashes and each earns $3 million. If one floods while the other holds back, the flooder earns $10 million and the loyal firm earns just $1 million. Reason it through as firm A. If B holds back, A gets $10 million by flooding versus $8 million by holding back, so A floods. If B floods, A gets $3 million by flooding versus $1 million by holding back, so A floods again. Flooding beats holding back no matter what B does, which makes it A's dominant strategy, and B thinks exactly the same way. So both flood and earn $3 million each, even though both would have earned $8 million by cooperating. This is the prisoner's dilemma, and it shows why an agreement every firm would benefit from tends to unravel: each partner's private temptation to cheat is stronger than its interest in the group deal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking oligopoly is defined by an exact number of firms, such as 'exactly two' or 'three to five.'
commonMistakes.correction: There is no fixed count. What matters is that firms are few and large enough to be interdependent, so each one's decisions noticeably affect the others.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming that similar prices across rival firms prove they colluded.
commonMistakes.correction: Prices can move together simply because interdependent firms watch and match each other, or because they face the same costs. Illegal collusion requires an actual agreement, not just parallel prices.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing a successful cartel is stable once the members agree.
commonMistakes.correction: Every cartel is undermined from within: each member can earn more by secretly exceeding its quota, so cheating is the norm and cartels tend to break down, as OPEC's history of overproduction shows.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing oligopoly with monopoly.
commonMistakes.correction: A monopoly is a single firm with no direct rivals; an oligopoly has a few rivals whose strategic interaction with each other is the central feature.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating collusion and cartels as normal, legal business coordination.
commonMistakes.correction: Explicit price fixing and output-restricting agreements among competitors are almost always illegal under antitrust law, carrying heavy fines and possible prison time.

compareContrast.distinction: An oligopoly has a few interdependent firms that must anticipate each other; a monopoly is one firm with no direct rivals to react to.
An oligopoly has a few large firms whose choices are interdependent; monopolistic competition has many small firms selling differentiated products, each too small to affect the others much.
Oligopoly firms are few and set strategy around rivals; perfectly competitive firms are many, sell identical products, and simply take the market price.
Colluding firms coordinate to cut output and raise prices toward the monopoly level; competing firms set price and output independently, which pushes prices down.

keyTakeaway: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large, interdependent firms, so each must act strategically around the others. They are tempted to collude to raise prices, but the prisoner's dilemma shows why each partner's incentive to cheat makes cartels unstable, and explicit price fixing is illegal on top of being fragile.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best defines an oligopoly?
options: A market dominated by a few large firms whose decisions are interdependent
A market with a single seller and no close substitutes
A market with many small firms selling identical products
A market with many firms selling slightly differentiated products
questionBank.explanation: An oligopoly is a market in which a few large, interdependent firms make most of the sales, so each firm's choices affect the others. A single seller (B) is a monopoly; many firms with identical products (C) is perfect competition; many firms with differentiated products (D) is monopolistic competition.
questionBank.skill: Defining oligopoly and distinguishing market structures

questionBank.prompt: Why must an oligopolist consider its rivals' likely reactions before changing its price, whereas a perfectly competitive firm does not?
options: Because oligopolists are legally required to notify competitors of price changes
Because a perfectly competitive firm has higher costs than an oligopolist
Because in an oligopoly there are so few firms that one firm's move noticeably affects the others, who will respond
Because oligopolists always sell identical products at a single fixed price
questionBank.explanation: Mutual interdependence is the defining trait of oligopoly: with only a few firms, one firm's price or output change materially changes rivals' sales, so rivals react and each firm must anticipate that. A perfectly competitive firm is too small to affect anyone, so it just takes the market price. There is no such notification law (A); the reasoning is about size and interdependence, not costs (B); and oligopolists often sell differentiated products and do not share one fixed price (D).
questionBank.skill: Explaining mutual interdependence and strategic behavior

questionBank.prompt: Two firms could each earn $8 million by holding output low, or $3 million each if both flood the market. If one floods while the other holds back, the flooder earns $10 million and the loyal firm earns $1 million. In this prisoner's dilemma, what is each firm's dominant strategy and the resulting outcome?
options: Hold output low; both earn $8 million because cooperation is rational
There is no dominant strategy, so the outcome is unpredictable
Flood the market only if it expects the rival to hold back
Flood the market; both defect and earn $3 million each, worse than cooperating
questionBank.explanation: Flooding pays more no matter what the rival does: $10M vs $8M if the rival holds back, and $3M vs $1M if the rival floods. So flooding is the dominant strategy for both firms, they both defect, and each ends up with $3 million, worse than the $8 million they would share by cooperating. Cooperation is jointly better but not individually rational (A); a dominant strategy clearly exists (B); and because flooding wins in both cases, it does not depend on predicting the rival (C).
questionBank.skill: Applying the prisoner's dilemma and identifying a dominant strategy

questionBank.prompt: OPEC assigns each member country an output quota intended to keep oil prices high, yet members have repeatedly produced more than their quotas. What does this pattern most directly illustrate?
options: That cartels are stable once members sign a formal agreement
That each cartel member has a private incentive to cheat, which makes cartels unstable
That OPEC operates as a perfectly competitive market
That raising output always lowers a single member's own profit
questionBank.explanation: A cartel holds output down to keep prices up, but any single member can earn more by quietly exceeding its quota and selling extra at the propped-up price. That private incentive to cheat is why cartels like OPEC are chronically unstable. A signed agreement does not make a cartel stable (A); OPEC is a cartel, the opposite of perfect competition (C); and cheating raises the cheater's own profit as long as others keep restraining output, which is exactly the temptation (D).
questionBank.skill: Diagnosing cartel instability from a real example

questionBank.prompt: In the 1990s lysine case, Archer Daniels Midland and rivals secretly agreed to raise the price of a feed additive; ADM later pleaded guilty and paid a $100 million fine, and executives were imprisoned. Under U.S. antitrust law, why was this arrangement unlawful?
options: Because the firms advertised their products too aggressively
Because the firms were too large to be allowed to operate
Because competitors agreed to fix prices, which is treated as almost always illegal price fixing
Because charging a high price is illegal for any single firm
questionBank.explanation: Price fixing, an agreement among competitors to raise, lower, or stabilize prices, is treated as almost always illegal under antitrust law, which is why the ADM conspiracy drew criminal penalties. Aggressive advertising is legal (A); being large is not itself illegal (B); and a single firm charging a high price on its own is not price fixing, which requires an agreement among competitors (D).
questionBank.skill: Connecting collusion to antitrust law using a real case

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement best defines an oligopoly?
options: A market dominated by a few large firms whose decisions are interdependent
A market with a single seller and no close substitutes
A market with many small firms selling identical products
A market with many firms selling slightly differentiated products
quickCheck.explanation: An oligopoly is a market in which a few large, interdependent firms make most of the sales, so each firm's choices affect the others. A single seller (B) is a monopoly; many firms with identical products (C) is perfect competition; many firms with differentiated products (D) is monopolistic competition.
quickCheck.skill: Defining oligopoly and distinguishing market structures

quickCheck.prompt: Why must an oligopolist consider its rivals' likely reactions before changing its price, whereas a perfectly competitive firm does not?
options: Because oligopolists are legally required to notify competitors of price changes
Because a perfectly competitive firm has higher costs than an oligopolist
Because in an oligopoly there are so few firms that one firm's move noticeably affects the others, who will respond
Because oligopolists always sell identical products at a single fixed price
quickCheck.explanation: Mutual interdependence is the defining trait of oligopoly: with only a few firms, one firm's price or output change materially changes rivals' sales, so rivals react and each firm must anticipate that. A perfectly competitive firm is too small to affect anyone, so it just takes the market price. There is no such notification law (A); the reasoning is about size and interdependence, not costs (B); and oligopolists often sell differentiated products and do not share one fixed price (D).
quickCheck.skill: Explaining mutual interdependence and strategic behavior

quickCheck.prompt: Two firms could each earn $8 million by holding output low, or $3 million each if both flood the market. If one floods while the other holds back, the flooder earns $10 million and the loyal firm earns $1 million. In this prisoner's dilemma, what is each firm's dominant strategy and the resulting outcome?
options: Hold output low; both earn $8 million because cooperation is rational
There is no dominant strategy, so the outcome is unpredictable
Flood the market only if it expects the rival to hold back
Flood the market; both defect and earn $3 million each, worse than cooperating
quickCheck.explanation: Flooding pays more no matter what the rival does: $10M vs $8M if the rival holds back, and $3M vs $1M if the rival floods. So flooding is the dominant strategy for both firms, they both defect, and each ends up with $3 million, worse than the $8 million they would share by cooperating. Cooperation is jointly better but not individually rational (A); a dominant strategy clearly exists (B); and because flooding wins in both cases, it does not depend on predicting the rival (C).
quickCheck.skill: Applying the prisoner's dilemma and identifying a dominant strategy

title: Monopolistic Competition
in30Seconds: Monopolistic competition is the market structure that describes most of what you shop at: many firms selling similar but DIFFERENTIATED products, with free entry and exit. Differentiation gives each firm a sliver of market power, so its demand curve slopes down and it can set price above marginal cost. Firms compete less on price and more on branding, quality, and variety. Short-run profit is possible, but free entry drives long-run economic profit to about zero. The catch: firms end up with excess capacity and price above marginal cost, so the market is not fully efficient.
whyItMatters: Restaurants, clothing labels, coffee shops, breweries, hair salons, app developers, and most consumer brands live in monopolistic competition, so it is the market structure that best fits everyday economic life. It explains why so much business energy goes into advertising, branding, and small product tweaks rather than price wars: a differentiated product is the only source of the modest pricing power these firms have. It also sharpens a policy debate you will meet again and again. Compared with perfect competition, monopolistic competition wastes some efficiency through excess capacity and prices above marginal cost, yet it hands consumers something perfect competition cannot: genuine variety and choice. Deciding how much that variety is worth is one of the recurring judgment calls in microeconomics.
learningObjectives: Define monopolistic competition by its three defining features: many firms, differentiated products, and free entry and exit
Explain why product differentiation gives a firm a downward-sloping demand curve and lets it set price above marginal cost
Distinguish price competition from non-price competition and give examples of branding, advertising, quality, and variety
Analyze how free entry and exit drive long-run economic profit toward zero at the point where perceived demand is tangent to average cost
Evaluate the long-run outcome: excess capacity and P greater than MC versus the benefit of product variety
Contrast monopolistic competition with perfect competition, monopoly, and oligopoly in one line each

collegeVersion.heading: What defines monopolistic competition
collegeVersion.body: Monopolistic competition is defined by three features working together. First, there are MANY firms, enough that each is fairly small and no one firm's decisions noticeably change what the others do. Second, and decisively, the firms sell DIFFERENTIATED products: goods that serve the same basic purpose but are distinct in some way buyers notice. Third, entry and exit are free, with no patents, licenses, or large barriers keeping newcomers out or trapping firms in. The name captures the mix. The 'monopolistic' part comes from differentiation, which hands each firm a small, private mini-monopoly over its own particular version of the product. The 'competition' part comes from the crowd of close substitutes just next door and the open door that lets still more of them appear. The theory was developed independently in 1933 by Edward Chamberlin, who published The Economics of Monopolistic Competition, and Joan Robinson, who published The Economics of Imperfect Competition — two economists arriving at the same idea in the same year. Think of the restaurants, clothing brands, coffee shops, and hair salons around you: many sellers, each offering its own recognizable take on a familiar product, and new ones always able to open.

collegeVersion.heading: Differentiation, market power, and a downward-sloping demand curve
collegeVersion.body: Differentiation is what separates this structure from perfect competition, where every firm sells an identical product and must accept the single market price. Because a monopolistic competitor's product is distinctive, some buyers prefer it specifically and will stay even if it charges a little more; if it cuts price, it draws some extra buyers away from rivals. In other words, the firm faces a DOWNWARD-SLOPING demand curve of its own rather than the flat line a price taker faces. That gives it a small amount of market power: it is a price setter, not a price taker, though a weak one, hemmed in by the many close substitutes. A firm can differentiate along four dimensions. Physical aspects are the tangible features an ad boasts about — a spicier recipe, a softer fabric, a redesigned interface. Location matters, as anyone who has paid more for coffee at a convenient corner knows. Intangible aspects include guarantees, reputation, and service. And perception, shaped heavily by branding, can make buyers treat near-identical goods as meaningfully different. Any of these can make a product distinctive enough to bend the firm's demand curve downward.

collegeVersion.heading: Choosing output: MR = MC, and why price sits above marginal cost
collegeVersion.body: Like every firm, a monopolistic competitor maximizes profit by producing the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost — the last unit whose extra revenue still covers its extra cost. But here the demand curve slopes down, and that has a crucial consequence. When a firm must lower its price to sell one more unit, the marginal revenue from that unit is LESS than its price, because the lower price applies to the earlier units too. So marginal revenue lies below the demand curve, and price is higher than marginal revenue. The firm sets output where MR = MC, then reads the price up on its demand curve above that quantity. The result is that PRICE EXCEEDS MARGINAL COST. That gap is the signature of market power: buyers pay more for the last unit than it costs the firm to make, unlike perfect competition where P = MC. The cost curves behind this decision — how marginal and average cost arise from fixed and variable costs — belong to the costs topic; this lesson simply treats them as the firm's given cost structure.

collegeVersion.heading: The long run: free entry, zero profit, and the tangency point
collegeVersion.body: In the short run a monopolistic competitor can earn an economic profit if price exceeds average total cost, or take a loss if it falls short — the same possibilities a monopoly faces. What changes the story is free entry and exit. When existing firms are earning profit, new firms enter with their own differentiated versions, and every newcomer pulls some customers away from the firms already there. Each existing firm's perceived demand curve shifts LEFT (and tends to flatten, as buyers gain more substitutes). New firms keep entering until that economic profit has been competed away to zero. When firms are losing money, exit does the reverse, shifting the survivors' demand curves right until losses disappear. Both forces converge on a distinctive resting point: the firm's demand curve just barely TOUCHES its average cost curve — the two are tangent. At that single point price equals average total cost, so economic profit is exactly zero. This is the same zero-economic-profit endpoint as perfect competition, reached by the same engine of free entry and exit. The difference lies in WHERE on the cost curve it happens, which is what the next section unpacks.

collegeVersion.heading: Excess capacity, inefficiency, and the payoff of variety
collegeVersion.body: Because the demand curve slopes down, it can only be tangent to the average cost curve on that curve's downward-sloping stretch — never at its very bottom. That has two consequences. First, the firm produces LESS than the output that would minimize average cost: it operates with EXCESS CAPACITY, the room it has to produce more cheaply per unit but no demand to justify doing so. The half-empty restaurant that could serve more meals at a lower cost per plate is the everyday picture of this. Second, price still exceeds marginal cost, so the last unit is valued by buyers at more than it costs society to make — the market underproduces relative to the efficient quantity. On both counts, productive and allocative, monopolistic competition falls short of the perfectly competitive benchmark. But the comparison is not one-sided. The very differentiation that creates the inefficiency also delivers something perfect competition cannot: real VARIETY. A world of identical products would be efficient and dull; monopolistic competition trades a measure of efficiency for the range of choices consumers actually enjoy. Much of the competition here is NON-PRICE competition — advertising, branding, quality, and service rather than price cuts — and advertising in particular aims to shift a firm's perceived demand curve outward or make it less price-sensitive, protecting the slim margin differentiation provides.

vocabulary.definition: A market structure with many firms selling differentiated (not identical) products, with free entry and exit, so each firm has a little market power but no lasting economic profit.
Making a product distinct from competitors' along physical features, location, intangible aspects like service and reputation, or buyer perception shaped by branding.
A good that serves the same basic purpose as its rivals but is distinctive enough that some buyers prefer it specifically.
The downward-sloping demand a single differentiated firm faces; because its product is distinctive, it can change price without gaining or losing all of its customers.
The ability to set price above marginal cost rather than accept a single market price; monopolistic competitors have a small amount of it.
Competing for customers through branding, advertising, quality, variety, and service instead of by lowering price.
The extra revenue from selling one more unit; when a firm must cut price to sell more, marginal revenue is below the price.
The point free entry and exit push a firm to, where its perceived demand curve just touches its average cost curve, so price equals average cost and economic profit is zero.

The gap between a firm's actual output and the output that would minimize its average cost; a standing feature of monopolistic competition because the tangency lies on the downward-sloping part of average cost.
Total revenue minus both explicit costs and implicit opportunity costs; zero economic profit means owners earn exactly their next-best return, a normal profit.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine a street with lots of pizza shops. They all sell pizza, but each one is a little different: this one has a wood-fired crust, that one has the corner spot, another has a logo everyone recognizes. Because your favorite is a bit special to you, it can charge a little more without losing you, so it has a tiny bit of pricing power that a plain corn-seller at a farmers market does not. If pizza shops are making good money, new ones open, and each new shop steals a few customers from the rest. That keeps happening until nobody is making extra money anymore. The shops survive, but each ends up a little emptier than it could be, and pizza costs a bit more than it strictly needs to. In exchange, you get lots of kinds of pizza to choose from.
eli10.analogy: A monopolistically competitive firm is like a food truck at a busy festival. Yours sells great tacos, so a loyal line forms even if you charge a dollar more than the truck next door. But nothing stops new trucks from rolling in, and each one that parks nearby shortens your line. Trucks keep arriving until everyone is just breaking even, and every truck ends up with a few empty spots it could have filled.
eli10.analogyLimits: The food-truck picture captures differentiation, weak pricing power, and free entry competing profit away, but it understates how strong the substitutes are: your festival taco feels quite unique, whereas many differentiated products are near-clones separated mostly by branding. It also does not show the cost curves that make 'excess capacity' precise — the empty spots are a loose stand-in for producing below minimum average cost.

workedExample: A coffee shop is monopolistically competitive: its location, blend, and atmosphere make it distinctive, so it faces a downward-sloping demand curve. In the short run it applies MR = MC and chooses to sell 180 cups a day at $4.50 each, while its average total cost at that volume is $3.50 per cup. Its economic profit is (P - ATC) x Q = (4.50 - 3.50) x 180 = $180 a day. Notice price ($4.50) sits above marginal cost, the mark of its small market power. That profit attracts imitators: new cafes open nearby, and each pulls a few regulars away, shifting this shop's demand curve to the left. Entry stops only when profit is gone. Suppose the shop settles at 120 cups a day at $3.75 each, where average total cost has risen to $3.75 too. Now profit is (3.75 - 3.75) x 120 = $0 — the long-run tangency. Yet its marginal cost at 120 cups is only about $2.50, so price still exceeds marginal cost, and it is brewing 120 cups when it could reach lower average cost at, say, 200 — that unused room is excess capacity. (Figures illustrative.)

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing monopolistic competition with monopoly because both names contain 'monopoly'.
commonMistakes.correction: A monopoly is a single firm with no close substitutes and lasting barriers to entry. Monopolistic competition has MANY firms and FREE entry; the 'monopolistic' label refers only to the small pricing power each firm gets from differentiating its product.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming that because firms have some market power, they earn economic profit in the long run.
commonMistakes.correction: Free entry competes profit away just as in perfect competition. In the long run economic profit is about zero; the market power only lets the firm set price above marginal cost, not keep a lasting profit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the long-run firm produces at the minimum of its average cost curve, like a perfectly competitive firm does.
commonMistakes.correction: Because demand slopes downward, it can only be tangent to average cost on the downward-sloping part, above the minimum. The firm therefore carries excess capacity — it produces less than the cost-minimizing output.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating advertising and branding as pure waste with no economic role.
commonMistakes.correction: Non-price competition is how these firms compete. Advertising can shift a firm's perceived demand outward or make it less price-sensitive, and differentiation is what gives buyers variety. Whether the spending is excessive is a separate, contested question.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing price equals marginal cost because the market looks competitive.
commonMistakes.correction: With a downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue is below price, and the firm sets output where MR = MC. So price ends up ABOVE marginal cost — the allocative inefficiency that separates this structure from perfect competition, where P = MC.

compareContrast.distinction: Both have many firms and free entry driving long-run profit to zero, but perfect competitors sell an IDENTICAL product as price takers (P = MC, no excess capacity), while monopolistic competitors sell DIFFERENTIATED products, set price above marginal cost, and carry excess capacity.
A monopoly is ONE firm shielded by barriers to entry and can hold economic profit indefinitely; monopolistic competition has MANY firms and free entry that competes long-run profit away.

An oligopoly is a FEW interdependent firms whose choices depend strategically on rivals' reactions, often behind entry barriers; monopolistic competition has many firms too small to be interdependent, with free entry.

Price competition fights for customers by cutting price; non-price competition — branding, advertising, quality, variety — is where monopolistic competitors put most of their effort, because differentiation, not a lower price, is the source of their pricing power.

keyTakeaway: Monopolistic competition is many firms selling differentiated products with free entry: differentiation gives each a downward-sloping demand curve and price above marginal cost, but free entry drives long-run economic profit to about zero at the tangency of demand and average cost — leaving excess capacity and some inefficiency in exchange for product variety.

questionBank.prompt: Which set of features defines a monopolistically competitive market?
options: A single firm protected by high barriers to entry, facing the whole market demand curve
Many firms selling differentiated products, with free entry and exit
A few interdependent firms whose pricing decisions depend on rivals' reactions
Many firms selling an identical product, each a price taker at the market price
questionBank.explanation: Monopolistic competition is many firms, differentiated products, and free entry and exit (B). Option A describes a monopoly, C describes an oligopoly, and D describes perfect competition — the three structures monopolistic competition is contrasted against.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the defining features of monopolistic competition

questionBank.prompt: Why does a monopolistically competitive firm face a downward-sloping demand curve rather than a horizontal one?
options: Because a regulator assigns each firm a fixed price it must charge
Because there is only one seller of the product in the entire market
Because firms secretly coordinate to keep the market price high
Because its product is differentiated, so some buyers stay when it raises price and it gains buyers when it lowers price
questionBank.explanation: Product differentiation means some buyers prefer this firm's specific version, so a small price increase does not cost it every customer and a price cut attracts some — a downward-sloping demand curve (D). A invents regulation not in the model; B describes a monopoly; C describes collusion, which is an oligopoly behavior, not what gives a monopolistic competitor its demand slope.
questionBank.skill: Explaining how differentiation produces a downward-sloping perceived demand curve

questionBank.prompt: A coffee shop with a differentiated product maximizes profit by producing where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. What does this imply about its price?
options: Price equals marginal cost, exactly as in perfect competition
Price equals marginal revenue, because the two are always the same
Price is above marginal cost, because a downward-sloping demand curve puts marginal revenue below price
Price is below marginal cost, because differentiation forces the firm to undercut rivals
questionBank.explanation: With a downward-sloping demand curve the firm must lower price to sell more, so marginal revenue is below price. Setting MR = MC therefore leaves price above marginal cost (C). A is the perfectly competitive result, which does not hold here; B is true only for a price taker; D reverses the logic — market power raises price above MC, it does not push it below.
questionBank.skill: Applying MR = MC to conclude that price exceeds marginal cost

questionBank.prompt: In long-run equilibrium a monopolistically competitive firm produces where its demand curve is tangent to its average cost curve. Because that tangency lies on the downward-sloping part of average cost, the firm:
options: Operates with excess capacity, producing less than the output that would minimize average cost
Produces exactly at the minimum of its average cost curve, like a perfectly competitive firm
Earns a large positive economic profit that persists indefinitely
Sets price equal to marginal cost, making the market allocatively efficient
questionBank.explanation: A downward-sloping demand curve can only touch average cost above its minimum, so the firm produces below the cost-minimizing output and carries excess capacity (A). B is the perfectly competitive outcome, which requires a flat demand curve; C is wrong because free entry drives long-run economic profit to zero; D is false because price stays above marginal cost, which is exactly the source of the inefficiency.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the excess-capacity result from the long-run tangency condition

questionBank.prompt: Several restaurants in a neighborhood are earning healthy economic profits. Under monopolistic competition, what happens over time and why?
options: The existing restaurants raise prices together and profits grow, because they act as one monopoly
New restaurants enter and pull away customers, shifting each existing firm's demand curve left until economic profit falls to about zero
Nothing changes, because differentiation lets each restaurant keep its profit permanently
The restaurants are forced to exit, because differentiated firms cannot survive competition
questionBank.explanation: Free entry is the defining response to profit: new differentiated competitors open, each taking some customers, shifting existing firms' demand curves left until profit is competed away to about zero (B). A describes collusion that free entry prevents here; C ignores free entry; D is backwards — entry, not exit, is the response to profits, and the incumbents survive at zero economic profit rather than being forced out.
questionBank.skill: Predicting the long-run entry response that erodes economic profit
